doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Race memory and prodigy children
summary: Swing Low Sweet Chariot, race memory and genes, and child prodigies: a nine-year-old alto player in New Jersey and a Cajun singing child.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Somebody told me, long years ago, that there was African chiefs that went down this great river in Africa and they sang a song that was the melody of “Swing Low Sweet Chariot.” And I read that in one of the history books that we have, out of our books at home. And I said to myself, why not?
Because remember it was part of that ritual.
They put them on the boat.
In the boat you know, and there’d be a falls — you know you put them in a river, then there’s a falls.
There’s a falls that they go down.
And as the boat would do this, then there would be an infection of the spirit of the person in the boat.

So they sang “Swing Low Sweet Chariot.” The melody. See the slave words, whatever they — is this, to me, is this a remembrance of that, brought here, and then they just put their words to it? But I’ll tell you it’s hard to say.
I refer to certain aspects, of like I think we all have what we consider an aspect of — not to minimize it — race memory.
I think it’s in the genes.
You think it’s in the genes?
I think there’s a memory that comes with all of it.

It’s like a recurring — because we have every — as it’s spoken of from a scientific point of view, even though we say we forgot, it’s still there. And then at the same time we say we forgot, then at whatever time it happens, we recall it. So that’s like telling us something. That what we think we’ve lost we haven’t lost. Truthfully it’s still there.
Otherwise what would you say to a person that’s three years old and writes all kinds of sonatas?
You know, like Mozart.
Right. What was he doing at five years old?

You’ve got to really think that that’s — and we saw a kid in New Jersey. He was about nine years old. And we were playing on the pier. And he was playing this — his mother and father brought him up to our group, “Our son can play the alto sax. Can he sit in with you?” And we say, “Yeah.” We always welcome. So he took his sax horn out of his case and put the mouthpiece on and I said, “What would you like to play?” He said, “Now Is The Time.” We said, “Okay, you set it.” He set it [scats] — and played Charlie Parker — and sound and all, everything that was Charlie Parker this kid played. I couldn’t believe it. We couldn’t believe it. And he was born to do that. He was born to do that. In fact, the guys took him aside and were talking mouthpieces with him and everything. I really wonder what happened to the kid.
And to watch his attitude was something. Because —
He was grown.
He was somebody, you know what I mean? Without a doubt. You watch him and you know he knows he’s somebody. I mean very big.
Yes. And he wasn’t a kid right off. He wasn’t playing like a kid.
Like a young soul with — like a young body with an old soul, that’s what I’m trying to say, you know what I mean?
We didn’t tolerate him. He tolerated us.
Because he took over.
He did. Into the band.
And righteously so. He rounded off everything, and hanging out.
Unbelievable.
No, it’s true.
Well when she mentioned that, this other kid popped to my mind. We just saw him on T.V. It was the kid that was doing the country thing with the little—
Oh, with the little accordion.
Concertina or something?
Yeah, and he was singing a Cajun song. Jim A Cajun song. And he was just singing — and then when he would [scats] when he would do that—
He was old.
He was as old as Methuselah.
And the time was just perfect.
And he was this high.
So where does he come from?
It’s amazing. You know he felt and knew what he was singing.
Yes he did.
Not just mimicking. Because there is that too. But he was in it.
It wasn’t Suzuki.
No definitely not.
No, that was too tough for Suzuki.
